title: Diffusion Isn't Just for Images — It Wants to Win Inference for Language Models
dek: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time, sequentially, and is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel at once, so the inference workload looks more like training — which is why Inception is betting on it.
why: A founding figure in diffusion models explains clearly why parallelism at inference becomes the deciding factor in architecture, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.
who: Engineers and founders focused on inference cost and latency-sensitive applications (voice agents, coding), plus AI investors who want to understand the architectural competitive landscape.
skip: The academic reminiscing at the start, 0:08–2:54, can be fast-forwarded; go straight to the architecture argument starting at 5:11.

points.h: Diffusion started because GANs were too unstable
points.body: Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then work in reverse to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

points.h: The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
points.body: Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters), got a diffusion model to match the quality of autoregressive models: the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but roughly 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still fairly academic, but it was enough to make him decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial scale.

points.h: Autoregressive inference is a memory bandwidth bottleneck
points.body: Ermon likens the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference the autoregressive model is still sequential — before generating the 10th token it must first generate all the preceding tokens. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth-bound; most of the time goes to moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

points.h: Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
points.body: Ermon points out that the economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by ‘the more parallel approach will eventually win’.

points.h: Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, mini
points.body: Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, and the mini nano series, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you cannot just run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang; you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't put it to use.

points.h: A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
points.body: Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, a reasoning LLM for tool calls, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served its LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM, because it could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to a fast model you can't go back, like broadband.

points.h: Diffusion is inherently more controllable than autoregressive
points.body: Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregressive has to wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it is aligned, what score the reward function gives it; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can tell whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is quite a bit of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some forms of guidance simply cannot be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

points.h: 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
points.body: Drawing on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.), Ermon estimates that roughly 20% to 30% of tasks care a lot about latency. As a lower bound, that share of the workload can be served by the model that delivers the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we are not yet at frontier intelligence, and much of the workload still needs frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

points.h: Flash Attention and DPO both came out of his lab
points.body: Ermon responds to the skepticism that ‘academia can't do large models’: the early diffusion work beat GANs at academic scale and was more stable, and later grew into Stable Diffusion and Midjourney; he also co-advised Flash Attention, and DPO originated from a project in his group and is now widely used to align LLMs and diffusion models. He argues academia's advantage is being able to make counterintuitive bets, having excellent students, and people not being afraid to take risks — many important AI ideas originated in academia.
